title: The Last Sands: first missions, a growing base, and a van with firing ports (Godot + Codex/Claude
author: DarthOrganism
selftext:
Hi everyone! It’s been a while since my last update, and I finally have quite a bit to share :)

I’m still working on The Last Sands, my desert post-apocalyptic game built with AI agents in Godot. Lately, more of the work has been about connecting things together: what you leave base for, who you take, and what changes when you get home.

The world has grown to include an old port, a ruined high-rise district, an adobe village, industrial sites and smaller roadside discoveries. Moving between them gives the landscape more variety, and also keeps finding new ways to punish my performance budget :)

A lot of time and effort has gone into **the terrain itself**: texture blending, decals, and transitions between sand, dirt, roads and the objects sitting on them. Getting those surfaces to meet naturally takes a surprising amount of iteration. It’s less obvious in a feature list than a new vehicle, but you see it everywhere you drive.

A few of the bigger additions:

* **Base buildings now visibly develop.** Workshops, barracks and supply facilities have different upgrade stages. Starting an upgrade puts scaffolding and materials on the plot; returning from an expedition reveals the finished building. Bringing resources home now leaves a visible mark on the place.
* **The first eight missions are in.** They introduce scavenging, combat, deliveries, rescuing survivors, upgrading the base and preparing a vehicle. They’re a small opening chain, but they give those systems a reason to interact.
* **A new crew van.** A lifted 4×4 with four seats, improvised armour, firing ports and an M2 mounted over the roof hatch. Getting everyone seated and shooting through the actual openings took some care.
* **More crew choices and abilities.** Grenadiers, engineers and a flamethrower-carrying chemist join the existing roles. More passengers also mean more water consumption. Character and vehicle ability trees add options including a combat drone and reinforcements.

Performance is still a recurring fight. As locations get denser, I keep revisiting streaming, terrain caching, static mesh merging, shadows and NPC updates. I’m checking repeatable driving routes and slow frames as well as average FPS.

One recent problem was particularly annoying: prepared terrain data worked in the editor, but the exported build generated different cache keys and rebuilt it. Fixing that meant digging into how source files and compiled scripts were identified. Quite a lot of work for an improvement you mostly notice by spending less time waiting.

The asset workflow is getting more disciplined too. New models reuse a shared material library and trim sheets, and I judge detail from the actual game camera. There’s now a registry so agents can find existing parts before making another version of something I already have.

Claude/Opus and Codex handle code and tooling, with Blender through MCP for modelling. My part keeps shifting toward setting constraints, reviewing results and deciding what actually belongs in the game. Each new feature brings another round of checking how it behaves with everything already there.
